articles.summary: Brazil’s decision to reelect leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva over Flávio Bolsonaro marks a setback in President Donald Trump’s bid to elevate like-minded leaders across the globe. The 80-year-old incumbent snatched victory from the jaws of defeat, blocked the rise of the far right and saved the planetary air-conditioning system of the Amazon from irreparable destruction . articles.summary: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva delivers a speech to supporters after winning the presidential runoff election in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 25, 2026. —Juan Barreto-AFP-Getty Images On Oct. 25, Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , won an unprecedented fourth term, defeating the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro with 51.79 % of the vote, a margin of nearly 4.4 million votes. For the 80-year-old Lula, who had trailed his opponent by 2.2 million votes in the first round of elections just three weeks earlier, the victory was a remarkable comeback. Brazil is the largest country and economy in Latin America, and the contest had become a test of whether the region’s rightward shift could be stopped. Lula’s victory interrupted that drift and dealt a setback to President Donald Trump’s ambition to build a hemisphere of governments aligned with his politics. Yet interpreting the result as a triumph for the left would be a mistake. articles.summary: Some Arab Americans who helped deliver Michigan to President Donald Trump in 2024 now say the Republican Party has abandoned its “America First” promises — and that Abdul El-Sayed is the candidate who actually represents them. The former Trump supporters say El-Sayed better represents the agenda they thought they were voting for — keeping American money at home and the country out of foreign wars. Their support could complicate Republican Mike Rogers’ efforts to preserve Trump’s gains among Arab American voters. A Washington Post-Schar School poll of Arab American registered voters nationwide, conducted in August and September and released this month, found that 58% favor Democrats for Congress, compared with 34% who prefer Republicans.
